paper_title: SepLLM Accelerate Large Language Models by Compressing One Segment into   One Separator
caption_used: Training loss curves over iterations for Vanilla, StrmLLM (n=64), and four SepLLM configurations. All models start with loss values exceeding 3.4 and converge as training progresses to 140,000 iterations. The Vanilla model achieves the lowest final loss at approximately 2.45, while StrmLLM (n=64) converges to roughly 2.60, showing a notable gap from the SepLLM variants. Among the SepLLM configurations, the H/T variant reaches the lowest loss at approximately 2.49, with SepLLM (n=128) settling at approximately 2.55, slightly above both the base SepLLM (n=64) and SepLLM (n=64, H) which converge near 2.51-2.52. The most rapid decrease in loss occurs within the first 20,000 iterations for all models, after which convergence slows considerably.
model_annotation: The graph displays training loss curves over iterations for five different models: Vanilla, StrmLLM (n=64), and four SepLLM configurations—SepLLM (n=64), SepLLM (n=64, H), SepLLM (n=64, H/T), and SepLLM (n=128). The x-axis represents the number of iterations, ranging from 0 to 140,000 in increments of 20,000, with the label "#Iteration". The y-axis represents the loss, scaled linearly from 2.4 to 3.4, with tick marks at intervals of 0.1. All models begin with a loss value above 3.4, and all curves exhibit a steep decline in the initial phase, particularly within the first 20,000 iterations. The Vanilla model (purple line) shows the most rapid convergence, reaching a final loss of approximately 2.45 by 140,000 iterations. The StrmLLM (n=64) model (blue line) converges to a loss of about 2.60, maintaining a noticeable gap from the SepLLM variants. Among the SepLLM models, SepLLM (n=64, H/T) (red line) achieves the lowest loss among them, settling at approximately 2.49. SepLLM (n=128) (dark blue line) converges to a loss of about 2.55, slightly higher than both SepLLM (n=64) and SepLLM (n=64, H) (green line), which stabilize around 2.51–2.52. After the initial rapid drop, all curves flatten significantly, indicating slower convergence as training progresses.
